newsitem.title: VATICAN: Anglican leader sees Henry VIII archive at Vatican.
newsitem.headline: Anglican leader sees Henry VIII archive at Vatican.

text.p: The head of the 70 million member worldwide Anglican Communion got a rare view on Wednesday of a letter from England's King Henry VIII which led to the birth of the Anglican Church more than four centuries ago.
Archbishop of Canterbury George Carey, paying an official visit to Pope John Paul, was on a tour of the Vatican's Secret Archives and St Peter's Basilica as part of his itinerary.
Archivists showed him a letter from 1530 in which Henry VIII asked Pope Clement VII to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon so he could marry the younger Anne Boleyn.
Clement refused, and four years later Henry issued the Act of Supremacy. It denied Papal jurisdiction and marked the founding of the Church of England, mother Church of the global Anglican Communion.
An official of the Secret Archives said that during the one-hour visit Carey was also shown letters written to various Popes by Mary Tudor and other European monarchs.
Papal primacy, or the recognition of the Pope's supreme authority over any unified Christian Church, is still one of the thorny issues testing the Catholic-Anglican dialogue.
The Pope said in a 1995 encyclical that for the sake of unity he was willing to seek an accommodation with other Christian denominations on the future role of the papacy.

Carey, on the second day of his official visit to Rome and the Vatican, also prayed before the tomb of St Peter and pronounced his first official meeting with Pope John Paul a success in their difficult dialogue on Christian unity.
"He told us he was very pleased (with the meeting)," Canon Jim Rosenthal, director of communications for the Anglican Communion, told Reuters as Carey toured St Peter's Basilica.
Carey, accompanied by his wife Eileen, knelt to pray before what archaeologists believe is the burial place of St Peter, the first Pope, directly under the basilica's main altar.
The Anglican leader visited the crypt where modern popes are buried. He stopped before the tomb of Pope Paul VI, whose 1963-78 reign coincided with the start of a Catholic-Anglican dialogue.
Carey met the Pope for a formal greeting on Tuesday night. At the end of the meeting, the Pope, Carey and other prelates delivered a group blessing.
"Also, we expect your blessing for Rome," the Pope told Carey in an impromptu remark. The future course of relations will be a topic of talks at an official audience on Thursday.
In formal speeches, both emphasised the drive for unity.

"Our churches bear the marks of separation and division," Carey told the Pope. "We cannot undo overnight doctrinal differences and the bitternesses that have resulted from the legacy of history but we are able to confront them as fellow Christians..."

Carey became Anglican leader in 1990. Two years later the Church of England voted to allow women priests in a move that severely tested relations between Canterbury and Rome. The first were ordained in 1994.
